newsitem.title: UK: Selling Western goods in India takes skill - report.
newsitem.headline: Selling Western goods in India takes skill - report.

text.p: India's vast population is luring Western companies eager to sell consumer goods to an increasingly prosperous middle class, but firms are learning that marketing is the key to success, according to a report published on Monday.

K.M.S. Ahluwalia, the founder of India's largest market research firm, ORG-MARG, said his mantra for Western clients is, "India is different, India is different, India is different," the Wall Street Journal reported.

India is benefiting from free-market reforms launched five years ago, and there is greater exposure to Western life -- with satellite television bringing programming such as MTV and Baywatch into more homes. But those changes have not swept away India's 4,000-year-old culture -- a culture where a natural frugality makes disposable consumer goods a hard sell, the newspaper's European edition said.

Ahluwalia said a recent survey of marketing managers by his firm showed that only 27 percent of food-company marketers said their expectations had been met. Of those selling consumer items, the figure was 33 percent, the Journal reported.
Even as Indians prosper, they remain frugal, refilling disposable cigarette lighters rather than throwing them away.
The lack of a social security system in India encourages a high savings rate. Despite a median annual household income of $480, the private savings rate is 24 percent.

But frugality is not the only issue Western firms must deal with. Food companies face the toughest challenges in country where traditional foods continue to reign, despite the popularity of American fast-food chains such as Kentucky Fried Chicken and Pizza Hut.

The key to finding a market for Western foods is pitching them as a snack rather than as a replacement for a traditional meal. "As long as it's a food for casual eating, you have a good chance of succeeding," Sunil Alagh, managing director of Britannia Industries Ltd, an Indian biscuit maker, told the newspaper. "When you try to get into the main meal, that's where you flop."
